Trying to Conceive

Fertility injections: why the strongest is not necessarily the right choice

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

When you have been trying to conceive for a long time, it is understandable to hope for the injection with the best and fastest result. Fertility medicines have made several forms of treatment possible, but there is no single strongest injection that suits every diagnosis. Some help follicles grow, some prevent an early hormone surge and others prepare the eggs for the next stage. Understanding those jobs is more useful than ranking the medicines by strength.

Start with the reason for treatment

Infertility can involve ovulation, sperm, the fallopian tubes or other factors. An injection that helps ovulation does not automatically overcome every possible cause. Your assessment and the proposed treatment (such as ovulation induction, intrauterine insemination (IUI) or in vitro fertilization (IVF)) determine which medicines may be useful.

The goal also differs between treatments. A clinic may aim for a limited follicle response in an ovulation-induction cycle, while an IVF cycle usually aims to develop several follicles for egg collection. More stimulation is therefore not always better. Medical history, ovarian reserve, previous response and risks all help shape the plan.

The hormone names explain different jobs

Follicle-stimulating hormone, or FSH, supports growth of the fluid-filled ovarian follicles that contain eggs. Luteinizing hormone, or LH, also participates in reproductive hormone activity. A natural LH surge helps trigger ovulation. Medicines may provide these hormones or hormone activity, or alter the signals controlling their release.

Gonadotropin-releasing hormone is shortened to GnRH. GnRH medicines act on the signalling system between the brain and ovaries. Human chorionic gonadotropin, or hCG, can mimic an LH-like signal for final egg maturation or ovulation. These are related parts of a treatment sequence, not interchangeable names for a pregnancy injection.

Buserelin: controlling the body’s own signals

Buserelin acetate is a GnRH agonist. After an initial stimulating effect, continued use can reduce the pituitary gland’s hormone signals. In some fertility protocols this helps prevent the body from ovulating before the clinic is ready, while another medicine stimulates follicle development. Suprecur is one example of a buserelin product.

GnRH-based suppression is also used in other gynecological care, including some endometriosis treatment, but formulation, indication and schedule matter. Do not transfer a prescription between purposes. Possible effects of suppression include hot flushes, vaginal dryness, headache, sleep or mood changes, altered sexual desire and breast discomfort. Following the schedule matters for timing; it does not establish a numerical multiplication of pregnancy success.

Menotropins or hMG: FSH and LH activity

Menotropins, also called menotrophin or human menopausal gonadotropin (hMG), provide FSH and LH activity to support follicle development. They are urine-derived preparations. Menopur is an example; in that product, hCG contributes substantially to the LH activity. The label’s activity description is more informative than assuming the preparation is simply equal amounts of two purified hormones.

These medicines can be used for selected ovulation problems and assisted-reproduction cycles. They are not a remedy for every reason the ovaries fail to respond. Headache, pelvic discomfort, nausea or local injection reactions may occur. Excessive ovarian response and blood-clot complications are important risks, but should not be described as ordinary discomfort everyone should expect.

FSH medicines: urinary and recombinant forms

Urofollitropin is a purified urine-derived FSH medicine. It is used to stimulate follicle growth in selected treatment plans. Older brand lists can be misleading because products, availability and formulations differ between countries. Check the active ingredient on the medicine you have actually been prescribed.

Follitropin alfa, found in products such as GONAL-f, and follitropin beta, found in products such as Puregon, are recombinant FSH medicines made using biotechnology. Both support follicle growth. Manufacturing and product characteristics differ, but alfa and beta are not labels meaning one is necessarily a stronger treatment for your situation.

The absence of LH does not by itself prove that an FSH preparation will produce a better pregnancy outcome. Nor should a purified urinary product be assumed to have fewer adverse effects in every patient. Your clinic considers the whole regimen and your response. An ineffective ovarian response cannot always be overcome by switching to a more expensive preparation or increasing the dose.

Lutropin alfa: LH for a specific need

Lutropin alfa is recombinant LH; Luveris is an example. Its licensed European use is alongside FSH for follicular development in adults with severe deficiency of both LH and FSH. It is not an injection everyone having IUI or IVF automatically needs, and it should not be described as a universal add-on for larger follicles.

Whether extra LH activity is appropriate is a specialist decision. The medicine belongs within a monitored stimulation plan, which carries risks including ovarian hyperstimulation. Ask what finding supports its inclusion in your own regimen and what the clinic expects it to change, rather than assuming an extra medicine must improve the result.

Cetrorelix and ganirelix: preventing an early surge

Cetrorelix, sold as Cetrotide, and ganirelix, sold as Orgalutran and other products, are GnRH antagonists. They block GnRH signalling and help prevent an early LH surge during ovarian stimulation. This supports the planned timing of maturation and egg collection; they do not serve the same purpose as the FSH that grows the follicles.

The start and finish dates depend on the protocol and response. Redness, swelling or discomfort at the injection site can occur. Headache, nausea or pelvic symptoms should be discussed according to their severity, and a possible allergic reaction needs prompt help. OHSS can occur during the overall stimulation cycle even when a medicine is being used to prevent premature ovulation.

hCG: the trigger stage

An hCG injection provides a signal that helps complete egg maturation and, in appropriate treatment, brings about ovulation. It is commonly called the trigger. In IVF, egg collection is carefully scheduled after the trigger and before expected ovulation. For other treatment, the clinic gives specific instructions about insemination or intercourse timing.

Urine-derived hCG and recombinant hCG are different preparations with related actions. Novarel, for example, contains urine-derived chorionic gonadotropin; it is not a brand of recombinant choriogonadotropin alfa. Do not substitute one product or device for another or convert units yourself. Exact administration timing can be especially important at this stage.

Choriogonadotropin alfa: a recombinant hCG option

Choriogonadotropin alfa, found in Ovitrelle, is a recombinant form of hCG used after the ovaries have been stimulated. Like other hCG triggers, it helps with final maturation or ovulation. It is a trigger option, not an alternative name for a daily FSH injection.

Being recombinant does not make it free of ovarian-hyperstimulation risk or universally safer for every person. Headache, nausea, abdominal discomfort and local reactions can occur. The clinic may choose a different trigger strategy or withhold a trigger when the ovarian response raises concern. That decision is made from monitoring, not from which preparation seems newest.

Monitoring is part of the treatment

Ultrasound tracks follicle growth, and blood tests may assess hormone levels. Your clinic uses the findings to decide whether to continue, adjust a dose, change timing or stop a cycle. A lower dose or a different schedule from someone else’s does not mean that your treatment is less serious or less carefully planned.

If too many follicles develop, proceeding can increase the risk of OHSS or multiple pregnancy. A cancelled cycle can be disappointing, but it may be an important protection. Follow the clinic’s advice about intercourse or contraception if a cycle is stopped; cancellation does not mean no eggs can be released. In IVF, embryo-transfer decisions also affect multiple-pregnancy risk.

Separate expected effects from warning symptoms

The exact adverse-effect list varies by medicine and formulation. Mild bruising, injection-site soreness, headache, breast tenderness or temporary nausea may occur. Buserelin and other suppressive regimens can also cause symptoms related to lower sex-hormone levels. Report troublesome sleep or mood changes rather than assuming they must simply be endured.

Increasing abdominal swelling or pain, persistent vomiting, rapid weight gain, reduced urine or difficulty keeping fluids down needs prompt contact with the fertility team. Breathing problems, chest pain, fainting, a painful swollen leg, or swelling of the face or throat requires urgent or emergency care. Severe symptoms are not evidence that the medicine is working especially well.

Why OHSS can need care after the injections finish

Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is an excessive response to stimulation. Enlarged ovaries and fluid shifts can cause bloating, pain and vomiting; severe cases can affect breathing and urine output or be complicated by a blood clot. This is different from a minor red patch at an injection site.

Symptoms may develop or worsen after the trigger or egg collection, and pregnancy can prolong them. Keep the clinic’s urgent contact information and follow the monitoring instructions after treatment as well as during it. If you attend another hospital, tell staff which fertility medicines you used and when. Do not delay care because the last injection was several days ago.

Make your medication instructions usable at home

Ask for a written schedule showing the active ingredient, brand, purpose, amount and time for each medicine. Have someone demonstrate the device and any mixing steps using the product you will receive. Confirm storage, expiry after opening, transport and disposal of used needles. Those details are product-specific.

If a dose is missed, the wrong amount is used, a pen seems faulty or you are unsure how much went in, contact the clinic. Do not double the next dose or repeat an uncertain trigger without advice. Mention all other medicines and relevant medical conditions, and keep the prescription list available when seeking urgent help.

Ask about outcomes rather than strength

Useful questions include: What problem is this medicine addressing? What response are we aiming for? What will the scans change? Which symptoms mean I should call? Ask how the overall plan relates to your chance of pregnancy and live birth, rather than judging success from the number of injections or follicles alone.

An early positive pregnancy test after an hCG trigger can reflect the injected hormone, so use the test date provided by your clinic. No injection guarantees conception. A plan can be reviewed after a cycle based on what was learned, without treating a disappointing outcome as proof that you should independently find a stronger drug.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

HFEA and ASRM distinguish diagnosis-specific stimulation, hormone control and triggering, with monitoring essential.

Regulatory and manufacturer product information identifies the active ingredients and indication differences; Novarel is not recombinant choriogonadotropin alfa.

RCOG describes OHSS warning symptoms and the need for specialist follow-up beyond the last injection.

How BeMama can help

All medicine groups in the source are restored with accurate roles, generic names, selected verified brand examples and explicit corrections to efficacy and adverse-effect claims.

When to seek help

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Stimulation medicines, suppressive medicines and triggers have different jobs.
  • All seven medicine groups need diagnosis-specific selection and specialist monitoring.
  • Recombinant production, a higher dose or an extra hormone is not a universal marker of better treatment.
  • Know the warning signs of OHSS and allergy, including after injections end.
  • Follow your own written schedule and ask the clinic about errors or substitutions.

Frequently asked questions

Which fertility injection is strongest?

There is no meaningful universal ranking. The appropriate medicine depends on its purpose, the diagnosis, your response and the risks of the whole treatment plan.

Are FSH and hCG injections the same?

No. FSH supports follicle growth, while hCG provides a trigger signal for final maturation or ovulation. They are used at different stages.

Why would I take a medicine that suppresses hormones?

Buserelin or a GnRH antagonist may help prevent an untimely hormone surge, allowing the clinic to coordinate stimulation and the next treatment step.

Is recombinant FSH always better than urinary FSH or hMG?

No universal advantage follows from manufacturing method alone. The clinic should explain the choice for your diagnosis and protocol.

Does everyone having IVF need lutropin alfa?

No. Its use is specific; the European indication includes severe LH and FSH deficiency with FSH treatment. Extra LH should have a reason in your plan.

Are Novarel and Ovitrelle the same ingredient?

Both provide hCG-related triggering action, but Novarel is urine-derived chorionic gonadotropin and Ovitrelle is recombinant choriogonadotropin alfa. They are not interchangeable without instructions.

Should I double a dose if I miss one?

Do not improvise. Contact the fertility clinic with the product name, intended time and what happened. Advice depends on the medicine and stage of the cycle.

Can OHSS happen after egg collection?

Yes. Symptoms can develop or worsen after treatment, especially if pregnancy occurs. Continue following the clinic’s warning and follow-up instructions.

Does an early positive test prove pregnancy after a trigger?

Not necessarily. Injected hCG can temporarily affect the result. Test when your clinic advises and follow its confirmation plan.

Why might the clinic stop a cycle that has many follicles?

An excessive response can make continuing unsafe because of OHSS or multiple-pregnancy risk. Follow the clinic’s advice even if stopping feels disappointing.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
